description: The CAT OS VARC content taxonomy. Every item in the corpus names WHY it exists in terms of these ids: the skill it trains, the reasoning pattern it exercises, the trap each wrong option is built from, and the difficulty dimensions it turns. The app's schemas enumerate these ids; tools/verify.mjs refuses an id that is not here; the skill ledger and the curator aggregate by them. Extend by adding ids, never by renaming one.

mastery_graph.description: Prerequisite edges, from the skill that should be settled first to the skill that builds on it. Derived from skills[].prereqs; listed here so a reader can see the ladders at a glance.

rc_question_types.label: main idea
rc_question_types.expert_move: Compress the whole arc into one sentence before the options; the winner must need every paragraph.

rc_question_types.label: title
rc_question_types.expert_move: A title is the main idea in six words; the same altitude rules apply.

rc_question_types.label: primary purpose
rc_question_types.expert_move: Name the verb: the author is arguing, questioning, reconciling, describing — then find the option with that verb and that object.

rc_question_types.label: author’s purpose
rc_question_types.expert_move: Ask what the author is DOING with this passage, not what it is about.

rc_question_types.label: author’s attitude
rc_question_types.expert_move: Collect the verdict words as you read; intensity and valence are two separate decisions.

rc_question_types.label: tone
rc_question_types.expert_move: Topic words set the subject; only judgement words set the tone.

rc_question_types.label: detail
rc_question_types.expert_move: Put a finger on the exact sentence; nearby truths are the decoys.

rc_question_types.label: EXCEPT
rc_question_types.expert_move: Find the three that ARE in the passage; the answer is what is left, and it is often plausible in the world.

rc_question_types.label: NOT true
rc_question_types.expert_move: Verify each option against the text; the false one usually shifts a scope or a direction, not a topic.

rc_question_types.label: phrase in context
rc_question_types.expert_move: Paraphrase the phrase from its own sentence before looking; the working definition is planted nearby.

rc_question_types.label: word in context
rc_question_types.expert_move: The sentence forces one sense; the dictionary’s commonest sense is the trap.

rc_question_types.label: inference
rc_question_types.expert_move: Only what the sentences force. Sensible is not the same as supported.

rc_question_types.label: implication
rc_question_types.expert_move: Take the author’s claim one honest step; the trap takes it three.

rc_question_types.label: must be true
rc_question_types.expert_move: Test each option: could the passage be entirely true and this option false? Then it is not forced.

rc_question_types.label: cannot be inferred
rc_question_types.expert_move: Three options are supported somewhere; the answer is the one whose support you cannot point to.

rc_question_types.label: author would agree
rc_question_types.expert_move: Separate what the author reports from what the author holds; agreement questions live on that line.

rc_question_types.label: application
rc_question_types.expert_move: Extract the author’s rule as a rule, then apply it mechanically to the new case.

rc_question_types.label: comparison
rc_question_types.expert_move: Find the sentence where the two things are actually compared; options invent comparisons the passage never made.

rc_question_types.label: strengthen
rc_question_types.expert_move: Name the assumption the argument leans on; the strengthener props it, the weakener kicks it.

rc_question_types.label: weaken
rc_question_types.expert_move: Find the link between evidence and conclusion; the weakener breaks the link, not the topic.

rc_question_types.label: assumption
rc_question_types.expert_move: Negate the option: if the argument collapses, it was a necessary assumption.

rc_question_types.label: paragraph function
rc_question_types.expert_move: Label each paragraph’s job as you finish it: sets up, attacks, replaces, qualifies, illustrates.

rc_question_types.label: why the author mentions
rc_question_types.expert_move: A detail is there to do a job for the claim around it; name the claim first.

rc_question_types.label: structure
rc_question_types.expert_move: Draw the skeleton — view, objection, turn, close — before reading the options.

rc_question_types.label: relationship
rc_question_types.expert_move: Two things in the passage: is one an example, a cause, a contrast or a qualification of the other?

rc_question_types.label: best characterisation
rc_question_types.expert_move: Characterise the passage’s move in a verb and an object, and check the option keeps both.

rc_question_types.label: scope
rc_question_types.expert_move: Mark the population, the period and the condition the author actually limits the claim to.

pattern_families.scope: Scope — how far a claim reaches
pattern_families.lang: Language traps — the small words that change everything
pattern_families.struct: Structural reading — how the passage moves
pattern_families.disc: Discourse — how sentences hold together in a paragraph
pattern_families.word: Words — meaning from context, parts and neighbours

reasoning_patterns.name: Explicit detail
reasoning_patterns.instinct: I can point to the sentence.

reasoning_patterns.name: Paraphrase recognition
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Different words, same claim — or same words, different claim.

reasoning_patterns.name: Central idea
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This is the sentence the others serve.

reasoning_patterns.name: Supporting idea
reasoning_patterns.instinct: True, and here to hold up something else.

reasoning_patterns.name: Purpose
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author wrote this TO do something; name the verb.

reasoning_patterns.name: Author’s intent
reasoning_patterns.instinct: What does the author want me to end up believing?

reasoning_patterns.name: Passage organisation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: I can see the skeleton under the prose.

reasoning_patterns.name: Reference tracking
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘This’ points at something; I know what.

reasoning_patterns.name: Reading for function
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Not what it says — what it is doing.

reasoning_patterns.name: Attention over a long passage
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The fourth paragraph counts as much as the first.

reasoning_patterns.name: Directly implied
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author all but said it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Strongly supported
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Two sentences together force this.

reasoning_patterns.name: Necessary inference
reasoning_patterns.instinct: If the passage is true, this cannot be false.

reasoning_patterns.name: Reasonable implication
reasoning_patterns.instinct: One honest step from the claim, not three.

reasoning_patterns.name: Inference versus speculation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Plausible is not the same as supported.

reasoning_patterns.name: Author’s view, applied
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author’s test, run on a case they never saw.

reasoning_patterns.name: Logical gap
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Something has to be true for that step to work.

reasoning_patterns.name: Author’s view versus reported view
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Whose view is this — the author’s, or the one set up to be knocked down?

reasoning_patterns.name: Premise
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This is offered as a reason.

reasoning_patterns.name: Conclusion
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This is what the reasons are for.

reasoning_patterns.name: Assumption
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Unstated, and the argument needs it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Qualification
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author limited the claim on purpose; keep the limit.

reasoning_patterns.name: Concession
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author granted this point without adopting it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Counterargument
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This is the other side, given its due.

reasoning_patterns.name: Rebuttal
reasoning_patterns.instinct: And here the author answers it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Causal claim
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Because — or merely alongside?

reasoning_patterns.name: Analogy
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Like this — in the one respect that matters.

reasoning_patterns.name: Generalisation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: From these cases to all cases — is that earned?

reasoning_patterns.name: Example
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This illustrates; it does not claim.

reasoning_patterns.name: Principle
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This is the rule the example serves.

reasoning_patterns.name: Evidence
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This is what is offered in support.

reasoning_patterns.name: Evidence versus conclusion
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Which sentence is the reason, and which is the point?

reasoning_patterns.name: Correlation versus causation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: They go together; nobody said one made the other.

reasoning_patterns.name: Description versus evaluation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author is describing this, not approving of it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Example versus principle
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The waiter is not the thesis.

reasoning_patterns.name: Necessary versus sufficient
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Needed for it is not the same as enough for it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Scope too broad
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The passage never went that far.

reasoning_patterns.name: Scope too narrow
reasoning_patterns.instinct: That is one paragraph, not the passage.

reasoning_patterns.name: Wrong population
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author said ‘some readers’; this says ‘people’.

reasoning_patterns.name: Wrong time period
reasoning_patterns.instinct: That was true then; the author does not say it is true now.

reasoning_patterns.name: Wrong condition
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The claim held only under a condition; the option dropped it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Wrong level of abstraction
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Same idea, wrong altitude.

reasoning_patterns.name: True in the passage, not an answer
reasoning_patterns.instinct: It is in the passage. It does not answer the question.

reasoning_patterns.name: Absolute versus qualified
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author hedged; the option did not.

reasoning_patterns.name: Some versus all
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘Some’ was the whole claim.

reasoning_patterns.name: May versus must
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The passage only says MAY; this option says MUST.

reasoning_patterns.name: Often versus always
reasoning_patterns.instinct: A tendency became a law.

reasoning_patterns.name: Implicit negation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘Hardly’, ‘far from’, ‘all but’ — the sentence points the other way.

reasoning_patterns.name: Double negative
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Not unlikely means likely; slow down.

reasoning_patterns.name: Comparative language
reasoning_patterns.instinct: More than what? Compared with whom?

reasoning_patterns.name: Temporal qualifier
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘Once’, ‘now’, ‘no longer’ — the claim is dated.

reasoning_patterns.name: Causal wording
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘Because’ is a claim; ‘alongside’ is not.

reasoning_patterns.name: Modal verbs
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Could, should, would, must — each is a different promise.

reasoning_patterns.name: Subtle negation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: One small ‘not’ reversed the whole option.

reasoning_patterns.name: Overstatement
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Right direction, wrong strength.

reasoning_patterns.name: Contrast marker
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘But’ is where the author starts speaking.

reasoning_patterns.name: Concession marker
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘Granted’, ‘to be sure’ — the author is giving, not claiming.

reasoning_patterns.name: Shift in tone
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The voice changed here; that is a signal.

reasoning_patterns.name: Pronoun reference
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Which ‘it’? Which ‘they’?

reasoning_patterns.name: Contrast
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Two things set against each other; find which one the author keeps.

reasoning_patterns.name: Continuation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This extends the last idea; nothing turned.

reasoning_patterns.name: Cause and effect
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This happened, so that happened.

reasoning_patterns.name: Problem and solution
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The trouble first, then what to do.

reasoning_patterns.name: Claim and evidence
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The claim, then what holds it up.

reasoning_patterns.name: Claim and counterclaim
reasoning_patterns.instinct: A view, and the view against it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Chronology
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Time is the spine.

reasoning_patterns.name: Analogy
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The comparison is carrying the argument.

reasoning_patterns.name: Definition
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author is fixing what a word will mean here.

reasoning_patterns.name: Example
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The general claim, then a case of it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Qualification
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The claim, then its limits.

reasoning_patterns.name: Pivot
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The passage just turned; everything before was setup.

reasoning_patterns.name: Conclusion
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The passage lands here.

reasoning_patterns.name: Transition
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The bridge between two movements.

reasoning_patterns.name: General to specific
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The claim, then the cases.

reasoning_patterns.name: Specific to general
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The cases, then the claim they add up to.

reasoning_patterns.name: Question and answer
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author asks it in order to answer it.

reasoning_patterns.name: View, critique, replacement
reasoning_patterns.instinct: A view is set up, taken apart, and replaced; the replacement is the thesis.

reasoning_patterns.name: Two views, adjudicated
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Two positions, and the author’s verdict between them.

reasoning_patterns.name: Phenomenon, then explanation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Something puzzling, then why it happens.

reasoning_patterns.name: History of an idea
reasoning_patterns.instinct: How the idea changed, and what the change shows.

reasoning_patterns.name: Predict before the options
reasoning_patterns.instinct: I know what the answer has to say before I read the choices.

reasoning_patterns.name: Systematic elimination
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Unsupported, then extreme, then reversed, then wrong scope.

reasoning_patterns.name: Attractive but unsupported
reasoning_patterns.instinct: I like it. The passage never said it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Recognising a weak distractor
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This one was never in the running.

reasoning_patterns.name: Eliminate without fully solving
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Three are gone; I can commit without proving the fourth.

reasoning_patterns.name: Deciding under time
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Ninety seconds. Choose on the evidence I have.

reasoning_patterns.name: Breaking a near-tie
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Two finalists; one word separates them; find it in the passage.

reasoning_patterns.name: Handling ambiguity
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The sentence allows two readings; the paragraph allows one.

reasoning_patterns.name: Recognising contradiction
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This option cannot be true alongside that sentence.

reasoning_patterns.name: Sustained attention
reasoning_patterns.instinct: I am still reading closely at line forty.

reasoning_patterns.name: Pronoun and antecedent
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This sentence cannot open: ‘it’ has nothing to point at yet.

reasoning_patterns.name: Demonstrative reference
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘This view’, ‘such cases’ — the thing referred to must already be on the page.

reasoning_patterns.name: Repeated noun
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The same noun, definite the second time.

reasoning_patterns.name: Lexical chain
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Word, synonym, hypernym — one idea walking through the paragraph.

reasoning_patterns.name: Chronology
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Then, later, finally — time orders the sentences.

reasoning_patterns.name: Cause then effect
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The effect cannot arrive before its cause.

reasoning_patterns.name: Contrast
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘But’ needs something to push against.

reasoning_patterns.name: Concession
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘Admittedly’ gives; the next sentence takes back.

reasoning_patterns.name: Example after claim
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘For instance’ follows the thing it instances.

reasoning_patterns.name: General to specific
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The wide sentence opens; the narrow ones follow.

reasoning_patterns.name: Specific to general
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Cases first, then the sentence they add up to.

reasoning_patterns.name: Definition then application
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The term is fixed, then used.

reasoning_patterns.name: Question then answer
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The question sentence comes first; the answer sentence cannot precede it.

reasoning_patterns.name: Claim then evidence
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The finding follows the claim it supports.

reasoning_patterns.name: Problem then solution
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Nobody solves a problem the paragraph has not stated.

reasoning_patterns.name: Rhetorical pivot
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The paragraph turns on one sentence; everything before is setup.

reasoning_patterns.name: Explicit transition
reasoning_patterns.instinct: ‘However’, ‘moreover’, ‘consequently’ — a signpost, with a direction.

reasoning_patterns.name: Implicit transition
reasoning_patterns.instinct: No signpost, but the idea handed on is unmistakable.

reasoning_patterns.name: Opening sentence
reasoning_patterns.instinct: It needs nothing before it, and names what follows.

reasoning_patterns.name: Closing sentence
reasoning_patterns.instinct: It hands nothing on; the paragraph lands here.

reasoning_patterns.name: Given then new
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The new information of one sentence is the given of the next.

reasoning_patterns.name: Parallel structure
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The same frame, twice — the second follows the first.

reasoning_patterns.name: Tense continuity
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The paragraph is in the past; this sentence is not.

reasoning_patterns.name: Stance continuity
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The paragraph is sceptical; this sentence is admiring.

reasoning_patterns.name: Topic progression
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Each sentence narrows or advances the one before.

reasoning_patterns.name: Scope continuity
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The paragraph is about one city; this sentence is about civilisation.

reasoning_patterns.name: Function of the missing sentence
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The gap needs a reason, an example, a turn or a landing — I know which.

reasoning_patterns.name: Competing endings
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Two sentences sound final; the one the other depends on comes second.

reasoning_patterns.name: Competing openers
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Two sentences could open; only one is free of references.

reasoning_patterns.name: Central versus supporting
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This is the point; that is what holds it up.

reasoning_patterns.name: Example versus claim
reasoning_patterns.instinct: A vivid story is never the point.

reasoning_patterns.name: Qualification kept
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The summary keeps the ‘only when’.

reasoning_patterns.name: Stance kept
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author was sceptical; the summary must be too.

reasoning_patterns.name: Certainty kept
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author said ‘may’; the summary may not say ‘will’.

reasoning_patterns.name: Nothing added
reasoning_patterns.instinct: If it is not in the paragraph, it is not in the summary.

reasoning_patterns.name: Compression
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Fewer words, same claim, same reach.

reasoning_patterns.name: Minor detail dropped
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The date, the name, the number — none of them is the point.

reasoning_patterns.name: Context clue
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The sentence tells me what the word must mean here.

reasoning_patterns.name: Morphology
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Prefix, root, suffix — I can build the meaning.

reasoning_patterns.name: Root family
reasoning_patterns.instinct: I know this root from three other words.

reasoning_patterns.name: Prefix logic
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The prefix sets the direction.

reasoning_patterns.name: Suffix logic
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The suffix sets the part of speech and the shade.

reasoning_patterns.name: Register
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Right meaning, wrong room.

reasoning_patterns.name: Connotation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Same dictionary line, different feeling.

reasoning_patterns.name: Near-synonym distinction
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Close, and the difference is exactly what is being tested.

reasoning_patterns.name: Confusable pair
reasoning_patterns.instinct: They look alike; the sentence wants one of them.

reasoning_patterns.name: Decoding an unfamiliar word
reasoning_patterns.instinct: I have never seen it, and I can still work it out.

reasoning_patterns.name: Polysemy
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This word has four senses; the sentence picks one.

reasoning_patterns.name: Tone carried by a word
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The author’s attitude lives in this one choice of word.

reasoning_patterns.name: The assumption gap
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Between the evidence and the conclusion, something unstated is holding the weight.

reasoning_patterns.name: Strengthen
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This makes the conclusion more likely, given the same evidence.

reasoning_patterns.name: Weaken
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This makes the conclusion less likely without denying the evidence.

reasoning_patterns.name: Flaw
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The reasoning would fail even if every premise were true.

reasoning_patterns.name: Resolve the paradox
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Both facts stay true; the option shows how.

reasoning_patterns.name: Inference from an argument
reasoning_patterns.instinct: What the statements together force.

reasoning_patterns.name: Principle
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The rule that, if accepted, justifies the conclusion.

reasoning_patterns.name: Parallel reasoning
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Same skeleton, different flesh.

reasoning_patterns.name: Evaluate the argument
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The answer to this question would decide whether the argument works.

reasoning_patterns.name: Find the conclusion
reasoning_patterns.instinct: The sentence the others exist for.

reasoning_patterns.name: Role of a statement
reasoning_patterns.instinct: This sentence is a premise for one claim and evidence against another.

reasoning_patterns.name: Sampling and generalisation
reasoning_patterns.instinct: From this group to that group — was the sample fit for it?

reasoning_patterns.name: Alternative cause
reasoning_patterns.instinct: Something else could have produced the same effect.

trap_families.scope: the option reaches further, narrower, or elsewhere than the passage
trap_families.direction: the option points the other way, or gives a view to the wrong owner
trap_families.support: the option is plausible but the passage does not support it
trap_families.relevance: the option is true but does not answer the question or plays the wrong role
trap_families.degree: the option is stronger or weaker than the text
trap_families.language: the option reuses the passage’s words or a near-synonym to smuggle a different claim
trap_families.tone: the option gets the attitude wrong in valence or intensity

trap_types.name: wider than the passage
trap_types.mechanism: generalises a specific claim into a universal one
trap_types.instinct: The passage never went that far.

trap_types.name: narrower than the passage
trap_types.mechanism: presents one paragraph, example or sub-point as the whole
trap_types.instinct: That is one paragraph, not the passage.

trap_types.name: the wrong people
trap_types.mechanism: shifts who the claim is about (some readers → everyone; experts → the public)
trap_types.instinct: The author said ‘some’; this says ‘people’.

trap_types.name: the condition dropped
trap_types.mechanism: drops the ‘only when’, ‘provided that’, ‘in cases where’ the author attached
trap_types.instinct: The claim held under a condition; the option lost it.

trap_types.name: the right idea at the wrong altitude
trap_types.mechanism: restates the idea one level too concrete or too abstract to answer the question
trap_types.instinct: Same idea, wrong altitude.

trap_types.name: the wrong time
trap_types.mechanism: moves a claim across time: what was true becomes what is; a prediction becomes a fact
trap_types.instinct: That was true then; the author does not say now.

trap_types.name: a comparison the passage never made
trap_types.mechanism: invents or reverses a comparison between two things the passage discusses separately
trap_types.instinct: More than what? The passage never compared them.

trap_types.name: points the other way
trap_types.mechanism: negates the author’s conclusion or flips the polarity of a relationship
trap_types.instinct: The author said the opposite.

trap_types.name: cause and effect swapped
trap_types.mechanism: keeps both terms of a causal claim and reverses the arrow
trap_types.instinct: The passage says A led to B; this says B led to A.

trap_types.name: the right view, the wrong owner
trap_types.mechanism: gives a position to the wrong party: the critics’ view to the author, the author’s view to the tradition
trap_types.instinct: Whose view is this?

trap_types.name: the view the author set up to attack
trap_types.mechanism: states, as the thesis, a position the author raised only to challenge
trap_types.instinct: That is the target, not the thesis.

trap_types.name: a criticism read as a rejection
trap_types.mechanism: turns the author’s qualified criticism into wholesale dismissal
trap_types.instinct: The author found a flaw; they did not throw the thing away.

trap_types.name: a concession read as the author’s position
trap_types.mechanism: takes a point the author granted to the other side as a claim the author holds
trap_types.instinct: The author conceded this; they did not endorse it.

trap_types.name: outside what the passage claims
trap_types.mechanism: introduces an idea plausible for the topic but absent from the text
trap_types.instinct: Where is this in the passage?

trap_types.name: true in the world, absent from the text
trap_types.mechanism: states something most readers already believe about the topic, which the passage never says
trap_types.instinct: I believe it. The author never said it.

trap_types.name: a reasonable guess the text does not make
trap_types.mechanism: takes the author’s claim two or three steps further than the sentences allow
trap_types.instinct: Plausible, but not sufficiently supported.

trap_types.name: true, but not enough
trap_types.mechanism: gives a real part of the evidence or reasoning as though it settled the question
trap_types.instinct: That is part of it; it does not do the job alone.

trap_types.name: a recommendation the author never made
trap_types.mechanism: turns a description or diagnosis into advice
trap_types.instinct: The author described it; they did not recommend anything.

trap_types.name: cause invented from correlation
trap_types.mechanism: reads ‘alongside’ or ‘associated with’ as ‘because of’
trap_types.instinct: They go together; nobody said one made the other.

trap_types.name: true, but not what was asked
trap_types.mechanism: accurate to the passage, but answers a different question than the stem asks
trap_types.instinct: True. Not an answer.

trap_types.name: the right idea, the wrong job in the argument
trap_types.mechanism: names real content but assigns it a different function (an objection called a concession; a setup called a thesis)
trap_types.instinct: Right fact, different job.

trap_types.name: an example mistaken for the point
trap_types.mechanism: elevates the most vivid illustration to the status of the claim it illustrates
trap_types.instinct: This is an example, not the author’s thesis.

trap_types.name: too absolute
trap_types.mechanism: applies always, never, only, all, none to a claim the passage qualifies
trap_types.instinct: The passage hedged; the option did not.

trap_types.name: right direction, too strong
trap_types.mechanism: intensifies the author’s claim without an absolute word: ‘useful’ becomes ‘indispensable’
trap_types.instinct: Right direction, wrong strength.

trap_types.name: right direction, too weak
trap_types.mechanism: softens a claim the author states firmly, or turns a conclusion into a mere possibility
trap_types.instinct: The author was sure; the option is not.

trap_types.name: may became must
trap_types.mechanism: converts a possibility, tendency or hypothesis into a certainty or a law
trap_types.instinct: The passage only says MAY; this says MUST.

trap_types.name: needed for it, read as enough for it
trap_types.mechanism: treats a necessary condition as a sufficient one, or the reverse
trap_types.instinct: Needed is not the same as enough.

trap_types.name: the right attitude, too much of it
trap_types.mechanism: keeps the valence of the author’s attitude and inflates its intensity (sceptical → contemptuous)
trap_types.instinct: Right side, wrong volume.

trap_types.name: the wrong side entirely
trap_types.mechanism: assigns the opposite attitude, usually by reading a reported view or a concession as the author’s
trap_types.instinct: Which side is the author actually on?

trap_types.name: attractive, but the passage never said it
trap_types.mechanism: offers a morally or emotionally satisfying statement with no support in the text
trap_types.instinct: I want it to be the answer. That is the warning.

trap_types.name: the passage’s words, bent
trap_types.mechanism: reuses the passage’s own phrases while changing the claim underneath
trap_types.instinct: Familiar words, new claim.

trap_types.name: a near-synonym that changes the claim
trap_types.mechanism: offers a dictionary sense of the word or a close synonym that the sentence does not support
trap_types.instinct: Close, and the difference is the question.

trap_types.name: sounds cleverer than the answer
trap_types.mechanism: dresses an unsupported or off-target claim in abstract, technical vocabulary
trap_types.instinct: Impressive is not the same as correct.

trap_types.name: right about half the passage
trap_types.mechanism: the first clause matches the text and the second clause swerves
trap_types.instinct: Read the second half.

trap_types.name: the right fact, the wrong reading of it
trap_types.mechanism: cites something the passage says and draws from it a conclusion the passage does not
trap_types.instinct: The fact is real; the meaning attached to it is not.

anchors.3: some CAT-list words, meaning recoverable from context
anchors.5: dense abstract vocabulary; several words the reader must decode
long periodic sentences with embedded qualifications
ideas about ideas; few concrete anchors
two or three steps, combining sentences from different paragraphs

anchors.3: one live finalist against the answer
anchors.5: two finalists separated by one word of scope or degree

anchors.3: the turn is present but quiet
anchors.5: the author’s position is carried by word choice alone
tight; the reader must decide on partial certainty

placement_traps.name: the pronoun bound to the wrong noun
placement_traps.instinct: ‘It’ has to point at the nearest thing that fits — and the wrong slot gives it the wrong thing.

placement_traps.name: fits its neighbours, breaks the paragraph
placement_traps.instinct: It reads smoothly here and makes the next sentence impossible.

placement_traps.name: the right topic, the wrong job
placement_traps.instinct: Same subject, but the slot needs a reason and this is an example.

placement_traps.name: closes the paragraph too early
placement_traps.instinct: A concluding sentence with two sentences still to come.

placement_traps.name: says again what the neighbour just said
placement_traps.instinct: The paragraph would say this twice.

placement_traps.name: widens or narrows the paragraph
placement_traps.instinct: The paragraph is about one case; this slot would make it about all.

placement_traps.name: contradicts the sentence beside it
placement_traps.instinct: Put here, the paragraph disagrees with itself.

placement_traps.name: changes sides
placement_traps.instinct: The paragraph is doubting; this slot would make it endorse.

placement_traps.name: the connective points the wrong way
breaks the time frame
placement_traps.instinct: Past tense paragraph, present tense slot.

placement_traps.name: introduces something never picked up
placement_traps.instinct: Nothing after it uses what it brings.

placement_traps.name: belongs in the paragraph, but not there
placement_traps.instinct: The sentence is needed — one seat later.

placement_traps.name: a summary where the paragraph is still building
placement_traps.instinct: The gap asks for the next step, not a recap.

placement_traps.name: a broad, quotable sentence the paragraph never needed
placement_traps.instinct: It sounds like a thesis; the paragraph already has one.

word_traps.name: a real sense of the word, not the one used
word_traps.instinct: Right word, wrong sense for this sentence.

word_traps.name: a near-synonym at the wrong strength
word_traps.instinct: Close in meaning, off in intensity.

word_traps.name: the same meaning with the wrong feeling
right meaning, wrong room
word_traps.instinct: This word belongs in a different kind of sentence.

word_traps.name: looks like a word it is not
word_traps.instinct: The spelling suggests a meaning the word does not have.

word_traps.name: the parts added up too literally
word_traps.instinct: The pieces mean that; the word has moved on.

word_traps.name: fits the word, not the sentence
word_traps.instinct: A meaning the word can have and this sentence cannot.

word_traps.name: the look-alike
word_traps.instinct: The other twin; nearly the same spelling, a different job.

word_traps.name: the opposite, dressed as the answer
word_traps.instinct: The sentence structure invited the reverse meaning.

word_traps.name: does not go with its neighbours
word_traps.instinct: The meaning is close; the words around it refuse it.

word_traps.name: the prefix read the wrong way

cr_traps.name: restates a premise
cr_traps.instinct: The argument already said this; it cannot be the assumption.

cr_traps.name: restates the conclusion
cr_traps.instinct: Saying the conclusion again does not support it.

cr_traps.name: does the opposite of what was asked
cr_traps.instinct: This weakens when I was asked to strengthen.

cr_traps.name: true and beside the point
cr_traps.instinct: Nothing in the argument turns on this.

cr_traps.name: shifts the argument’s scope
cr_traps.instinct: The argument was about this group; the option is about another.

cr_traps.name: supports the wrong link
cr_traps.instinct: This props a premise, not the step from premise to conclusion.

cr_traps.name: explains one fact, not the tension
cr_traps.instinct: Both facts have to stay true; this only accounts for one.

cr_traps.name: shares the topic, not the structure
denies the evidence instead of the reasoning
cr_traps.instinct: A flaw lives in the step, not in the facts.

cr_traps.name: ignores another cause
cr_traps.instinct: Something else could have done it.

audit_targets.answer_key_tolerance: no letter above 32% or below 18% of keys within any type, computed over the whole corpus
audit_targets.trap_dominance: no single trap type above 20% of a type’s distractors
audit_targets.inference_share_rc: between 35% and 55% of RC questions in the inference family
audit_targets.option_length_ratio: longest option at most 1.9 times the shortest within a question
audit_targets.absolute_language_bias: the fraction of correct options containing an absolute word must be within 0.5 to 2 times the fraction among distractors
